clue.text: Stuffy clubs fail to win

parts.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs
to fail to win a game is to be beaten

explanation.surface: A gloomy card player complains that clubs are a losing hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A close room or day is airless and humid, which is what stuffy describes.

clue.text: Big cheese from France arrived right on time to accept honour

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so the honour goes inside

parts.note: past tense of come
Member of the Order of the British Empire, a British honour
R abbreviates right
T abbreviates time

explanation.surface: An important Frenchman turns up punctually to receive an award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big cheese' looks like a VIP, but here it is literal: a large French cheese. The MBE is a British honour awarded by the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Camembert is a large soft round cheese from Normandy in France.

clue.text: Outstanding victory, blocking defensive blunder

indicators.note: something blocking a gap stands inside it, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: an own goal, a football defender's error
a win is a victory

explanation.surface: A football match report: a superb win despite a defensive howler.
explanation.definitionFit: A debt that is outstanding is still owing, in the sense of unpaid.

clue.text: Feeling cold, having abandoned Smiley?

indicators.note: what is abandoned is left behind, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: a smiley face drawn with keyboard characters
C for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Someone feels chilly having left their friend Smiley behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Smiley looks like a name, perhaps le Carré's spy, but it is the keyboard face.
explanation.definitionFit: An emotion is a feeling such as joy or anger; the words are synonyms.

clue.text: Meeting René, retired nobleman in residence

indicators.note: someone in residence lives inside a place, so one piece sits within the other
to retire is to withdraw or go back, so the name is read backwards

parts.note: the French name taken as written
a count is a European nobleman

explanation.surface: A retired French aristocrat called René is visited at his stately home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' reads as the nobleman's status, but it turns the name round; 'in residence' then places the nobleman inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An encounter is a meeting, especially a chance or unexpected one.

clue.text: Last bear

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to continue or survive over time
second meaning: to put up with something unpleasant

explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like adjective and noun, as in the last bear alive; both are verbs here.
explanation.definitionFit: To endure is both to persist over time and to tolerate hardship, matching each verb.

clue.text: Rum, cigar and some sensible knitwear

indicators.note: rum in British usage means odd or strange, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A cosy evening of rum, a cigar and a practical woolly jumper.
explanation.definitionFit: A cardigan is a knitted jumper that buttons at the front, a practical item of woollen clothing.

clue.text: Several upper-class chaps keeping pet cuckoo

parts.note: U is the old label for upper-class usage

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so a piece goes within

parts.note: chaps are men

indicators.note: cuckoo means crazy, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A number of posh gentlemen keep a pet bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cuckoo' looks like the pet bird itself; it signals the rearrangement of pet.
explanation.definitionFit: Umpteen is an informal word for a large but unspecified number, loosely matching several.

clue.text: Shabby stuff found in dissertations in America

definitions.note: a phrase meaning the place; the answer names America itself

indicators.note: a thing found in another is contained by it, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: theses are academic dissertations
tat is cheap, tasteless goods

explanation.surface: An academic complains about poor work in American dissertations.
explanation.definitionFit: The States is an informal name for the United States, so being there is being in America.

clue.text: Major US tycoon admits lacking practice

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the phrase holds the answer within it

parts.note: letters spanning the three words

explanation.surface: A big American business magnate confesses he is out of practice.
explanation.definitionFit: Skills that are rusty have deteriorated through lack of use, like metal left idle.

clue.text: Goods delivered by post Liam sent back direct

indicators.note: something sent back returns the way it came, so the name runs from end to start

parts.note: the man's name taken as written
to direct someone is to order them

explanation.surface: Liam is told to return a parcel that arrived through the post.
explanation.definitionFit: Mail order is the trade of buying goods from a catalogue and having them posted, so it names such goods loosely.

clue.text: Iron the newspapers

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to smooth clothes flat with heat
second meaning: journalists and their publications collectively

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like an instruction to iron the papers, as a butler once did; the two parts are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: To press a shirt is to iron it, and the press is the collective term for newspapers and reporters.

clue.text: More sultry island circled by criminal

indicators.note: a thing circled by another is ringed round, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a mugger is a street robber
I is the map abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A humid tropical island is surrounded by lawless types.
explanation.definitionFit: Muggy weather is warm and damp, so muggier is the comparative of sultry.

clue.text: I write back at play occasionally, in a cack-handed way

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: going back means reading the word for writing from right to left

parts.note: to pen a letter is to write it

indicators.note: something done occasionally happens now and then, so only every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A writer confesses to producing clumsy work now and then while at leisure.
explanation.walkthrough: Cack-handed is British slang for clumsy.
explanation.definitionFit: Inept means lacking skill, so ineptly is a synonym for clumsily, or cack-handedly.

clue.text: Merry Santa, completely naked, wandering in search of adventure

indicators.note: stripped completely naked, each word loses its outer layer at both ends

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters
the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A jolly Father Christmas strips off and roams about looking for excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: Both Merry and Santa lose their first and last letters, leaving ERR and ANT.
explanation.definitionFit: A knight errant was one who roamed in quest of adventures, the original sense of the word.

clue.text: Maybe Tommy playing poker with Cora

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are toyed with and rearranged

parts.note: the letters of poker and Cora, with joining them

explanation.surface: Tommy sits down to a card game with Cora.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' just joins the two words of fodder. Tommy is The Who's 1969 album about a pinball-playing boy.
explanation.definitionFit: Tommy is the famous rock opera by The Who, so it is an example signalled by Maybe.

clue.text: Attractive periodical — 1 cent on Web

parts.note: a mag is short for magazine
the Web and the Net both name the internet
the Roman numeral for one
C is the abbreviation for cent

explanation.surface: A handsome magazine costs a single cent online.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' places the numeral and cent after the Web piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnetic personality draws people in, a figurative sense of attractive borrowed from magnets.

clue.text: See throne here?

parts.note: surface reading: an invitation to view a monarch's seat somewhere
setter's reading: a see is a bishop's diocese, whose principal church houses the bishop's throne

explanation.walkthrough: A bishop's seat is called a cathedra, Latin for chair, and the church containing it gives the diocese, or see, its centre.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal church of a diocese, holding the bishop's official chair, so where see and throne meet.

clue.text: Perform good joke about Yankee bishop — his best friend might get it after dinner

definitions.text: his best friend might get it after dinner

indicators.note: about means around, so the joke word surrounds the other pieces

parts.note: to do is to perform
G abbreviates good
a gag is a joke
Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A comedy routine about an American churchman, ending with leftovers for his pet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'his' refers back to the bishop; man's best friend is the dog, who gets the restaurant leftovers taken home.
explanation.definitionFit: A doggy bag holds a diner's leftovers to take home, notionally for the dog.

clue.text: Tubby friar's bound to get his sweets here!

definitions.text: Tubby friar's bound to get his sweets here!

parts.words: Tubby friar's bound to get his sweets here!
parts.note: surface reading: a plump monk is sure to visit the place selling sweets
setter's reading: the plump friar of Robin Hood legend owns the store, so the place is named after him

explanation.walkthrough: Robin Hood's portly companion is Friar Tuck; in British schools a tuck shop is the kiosk selling sweets and snacks, tuck being slang for food.
explanation.definitionFit: A British school snack kiosk where pupils buy confectionery, here pictured as the friar's own store.

clue.text: Agitate to kettle Resistance — put one's foot in it!

indicators.note: police kettle a crowd by penning it in, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: to stir up is to agitate
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: Protest organisers are hemmed in by police and someone makes a gaffe.
explanation.walkthrough: Kettling is the British police tactic of corralling protesters. 'put one's foot in it' looks like a blunder but is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A stirrup is the loop hanging from a saddle into which a rider literally places a foot.

clue.text: That's part of the West Country sorted out!

indicators.note: sorted out suggests letters rearranged into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A cheerful declaration that a problem in the south-west of England has been fixed.
explanation.walkthrough: The West Country is the south-west of England; Dorset is a county there.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorset is an English county on the south coast, one of the counties making up that region.

clue.text: To argue violently is an atrocious act

indicators.note: violence throws things about, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A moral claim that fierce arguing is itself a terrible deed.
explanation.definitionFit: An outrage is a shocking, wicked act, so a synonym for an atrocity.

clue.text: Stump Ireland's official ensuring fair play

parts.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A cricket match: Ireland's wicket and the official watching over it.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no separate signal here; the letters sit in plain view across Stump and Ireland's, and the cricket stumps fit the umpire's scene.
explanation.definitionFit: An umpire is the official who enforces the rules in cricket, tennis and baseball.

clue.text: Running, loudly making a noise like a cow

parts.note: f, forte, is the musical marking for loud

parts.words: making a noise like a cow
parts.note: cattle are said to low

explanation.surface: A cow bellows while galloping across a field.
explanation.definitionFit: Running water is flowing water; both describe a steady moving stream.

clue.text: Sounds like free money for Federer!

indicators.note: sounds like says the answer is said the same as another word

parts.note: frank means free and open in speech

explanation.surface: An exclamation that tennis star Roger Federer gets cash for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Federer is Swiss, and Switzerland still uses the franc.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swiss franc is the currency of Switzerland, so it is the money Federer would use at home.

clue.text: Artist pal orbiting space station

indicators.note: a body orbiting something travels round it, so one piece encircles the other

parts.note: a mate is a friend
the International Space Station

explanation.surface: An artist's friend is circling the Earth aboard the space station.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Matisse was a French painter, a leading figure of Fauvism, so he is an example of an artist.

clue.text: To save money, do winter sport when the afternoon is over

parts.note: to ski is to do a winter sport

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so the abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: p.m. marks afternoon hours

explanation.surface: A thrifty holidaymaker hits the slopes only once the afternoon has finished.
explanation.definitionFit: To skimp is to economise by spending or using less than needed.

clue.text: In the morning, exercise exhausted king, a ruler in the Middle East

definitions.text: a ruler in the Middle East

parts.note: a.m. marks the morning hours

indicators.note: an exhausted thing has had its insides used up, so only its two ends remain

parts.note: the first and last letters
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A Gulf monarch is worn out by his morning workout.
explanation.definitionFit: Ameer is a variant spelling of emir, the title of a Muslim ruler or commander.

clue.text: British kit commercial that is beginning to rile army bod

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British
rig is gear or equipment
an advertisement
i.e., id est, means that is

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter alone

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: An advert for British military gear starts to annoy a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: Bod is British slang for a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A brigadier is a senior army officer commanding a brigade, so a particular army person.

clue.text: Politician introduced to fresh ganache, a French speciality

indicators.note: something introduced to a mixture is put into it, so one piece goes inside
fresh means new, so the letters are made into a new arrangement

parts.note: the chocolate filling, taken as written
Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician is served a freshly made chocolate dessert from France.
explanation.definitionFit: Champagne is sparkling wine made only in that region of France, a famous national product.

clue.text: Kick out former partner, sport student

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
physical education, school sport
L for learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: Someone throws out an old flame who is a sports student.
explanation.definitionFit: To expel a pupil is to throw them out of school, the idiom kick out.
